### Chapter 15: Hierarchical and Sleeve-Based Allocation {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: sol-15-setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
library(knitr)

R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
Re <- R - rf
stopifnot(ncol(Re) == 16L, !anyNA(Re))
N  <- ncol(Re)

# The chapter's sleeves, moments and helpers, repeated so that this fragment
# runs on its own.
sleeve_of <- function(a) dplyr::case_when(
  grepl("_equity$", a)     ~ "equity",
  grepl("_government$", a) ~ "government",
  grepl("_credit$", a)     ~ "credit",
  TRUE                     ~ "commodity")
sleeves <- split(colnames(Re), sleeve_of(colnames(Re)))
stopifnot(setequal(unlist(sleeves), colnames(Re)))

S    <- stats::cov(Re)
same <- outer(sleeve_of(colnames(S)), sleeve_of(colnames(S)), "==")
stopifnot(all(dim(same) == dim(S)), isSymmetric(same))
S_block <- S; S_block[!same] <- 0

gmv_qp <- function(S) {
  n   <- ncol(S)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(rep(1, n), diag(n)),
                            bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(S))
}
mu    <- colMeans(Re)
p_vol <- function(w) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w)) * sqrt(12)
p_ret <- function(w) sum(mu * w) * 12
p_sr  <- function(w) p_ret(w) / p_vol(w)
eff_bets <- function(w) 1 / sum(w^2)

within_gmv <- function(S, sleeves) lapply(sleeves, function(a)
  if (length(a) == 1L) setNames(1, a) else gmv_qp(S[a, a]))
unroll <- function(b, v) {
  stopifnot(identical(names(b), names(v)))
  w <- unlist(lapply(names(v), function(k) b[[k]] * v[[k]]))
  w[colnames(Re)]
}

# Hierarchical risk parity, single linkage, as in the chapter's box.
D  <- sqrt(0.5 * (1 - stats::cor(Re)))
hc <- hclust(stats::as.dist(D), method = "single")
ord <- colnames(Re)[hc$order]
hrp <- function(S, ord) {
  iv_var <- function(items) {
    s <- S[items, items, drop = FALSE]; iv <- 1 / diag(s); iv <- iv / sum(iv)
    as.numeric(t(iv) %*% s %*% iv)
  }
  w <- setNames(rep(1, length(ord)), ord)
  clusters <- list(ord)
  while (length(clusters)) {
    nxt <- list()
    for (cl in clusters) {
      if (length(cl) < 2L) next
      h <- floor(length(cl) / 2); a <- cl[1:h]; b <- cl[(h + 1):length(cl)]
      alpha <- 1 - iv_var(a) / (iv_var(a) + iv_var(b))
      w[a] <- w[a] * alpha; w[b] <- w[b] * (1 - alpha)
      nxt <- c(nxt, list(a), list(b))
    }
    clusters <- nxt
  }
  w[colnames(S)]
}
w_hrp <- hrp(S, ord)

# The by-hand proxy of the chapter, with the training period as an argument.
three <- sleeves[c("equity", "government", "credit")]
proxy_by_hand <- function(a, W = 60L) {
  X <- zoo::coredata(Re[, a, drop = FALSE]); n <- nrow(X); out <- numeric(n)
  w <- rep(1 / length(a), length(a))                  # the back-fill: equal, then drifting
  for (t in seq_len(W)) {
    out[t] <- sum(w * X[t, ]); w <- w * (1 + X[t, ]) / (1 + out[t])
  }
  for (t in (W + 1):n)                                # then rolling minimum variance
    out[t] <- sum(gmv_qp(stats::cov(X[(t - W):(t - 1), ])) * X[t, ])
  out
}
by_hand <- sapply(three, proxy_by_hand)
b_hand  <- gmv_qp(stats::cov(by_hand))

# The out-of-sample race of the chapter.
FIRST_OOS <- 121L                                # the register's first out-of-sample month
stopifnot(FIRST_OOS == which(model_year(zoo::index(Re)) == 11L)[1])   # first month of model year 11
oos    <- FIRST_OOS:nrow(Re)
rf_oos <- rf[oos]
Xm <- zoo::coredata(Re); Rm <- zoo::coredata(R)

race <- function(W) {
  paths <- lapply(oos, function(t) {
    X  <- Xm[(t - W):(t - 1), ]                    # the W months before t, nothing after
    Sw <- stats::cov(X)
    v  <- within_gmv(Sw, sleeves)
    sr <- sapply(names(v), function(k) X[, sleeves[[k]], drop = FALSE] %*% v[[k]])
    Sb <- Sw; Sb[!same] <- 0
    rbind(flat           = gmv_qp(Sw),
          nested         = unroll(gmv_qp(stats::cov(sr)), v),
          `block-diagonal` = gmv_qp(Sb),
          `equal weight` = rep(1 / N, N))
  })
  strategies <- rownames(paths[[1]])
  ret  <- sapply(strategies, function(s) vapply(seq_along(oos), function(i)
    sum(paths[[i]][s, ] * Rm[oos[i], ]), numeric(1)))
  turn <- sapply(strategies, function(s) {
    eop <- rep(0, N); out <- numeric(length(oos))
    for (i in seq_along(oos)) {
      w <- paths[[i]][s, ]; r <- Rm[oos[i], ]
      out[i] <- 0.5 * sum(abs(w - eop)); eop <- w * (1 + r) / (1 + sum(w * r))
    }
    mean(out) * 12
  })
  list(ret = ret, turnover = turn,
       sleeve_budget = sapply(seq_along(oos), function(i)
         tapply(paths[[i]]["nested", ], sleeve_of(colnames(Re)), sum)))
}
oos_stats <- function(r) {
  n  <- length(r)
  ar <- prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - 1
  af <- prod(1 + rf_oos)^(12 / n) - 1
  v  <- stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12)
  c(ann_return = ar, ann_vol = v, sharpe = (ar - af) / v)
}
race60  <- race(60L)
stats60 <- t(apply(race60$ret, 2, oos_stats))
```

#### Exercise 1

`race()` reads the partition from `sleeves` and `same`, so the currency
hierarchy is a matter of replacing those two objects, running the race, and
putting the class partition back.

```{r}
#| label: sol-15-ex1
currency_of <- function(a) sub("_.*$", "", a)              # US, UK, EU, CH, JP, GLOBAL
class_partition <- list(sleeves = sleeves, same = same)
sleeves <- split(colnames(Re), currency_of(colnames(Re)))
same    <- outer(currency_of(colnames(Re)), currency_of(colnames(Re)), "==")
stopifnot(setequal(unlist(sleeves), colnames(Re)), length(sleeves) == 6L)
race60_ccy  <- race(60L)
stats60_ccy <- t(apply(race60_ccy$ret, 2, oos_stats))
sleeves <- class_partition$sleeves; same <- class_partition$same
stopifnot(identical(names(sleeves), c("commodity", "credit", "equity", "government")),
          identical(race60_ccy$ret[, "flat"], race60$ret[, "flat"]))  # flat ignores the partition

ex1 <- rbind(flat                       = stats60["flat", ],
             `nested, class sleeves`    = stats60["nested", ],
             `nested, currency sleeves` = stats60_ccy["nested", ],
             `block-diagonal, class`    = stats60["block-diagonal", ],
             `block-diagonal, currency` = stats60_ccy["block-diagonal", ],
             `equal weight`             = stats60["equal weight", ])
# What the prose states: the currency hierarchy has the higher Sharpe ratio and
# return but not the lower volatility, so it does not dominate; flat dominates both.
stopifnot(stats60_ccy["nested", "sharpe"]     > stats60["nested", "sharpe"],
          stats60_ccy["nested", "ann_return"] > stats60["nested", "ann_return"],
          stats60_ccy["nested", "ann_vol"]    > stats60["nested", "ann_vol"],
          all(stats60["flat", "ann_return"] > ex1[c(2, 3), "ann_return"]),
          all(stats60["flat", "ann_vol"]    < ex1[c(2, 3), "ann_vol"]))
round(ex1, 4)
```

The currency hierarchy is the more efficient of the two without dominating
the class hierarchy: a Sharpe ratio of
`r sprintf("%.3f", stats60_ccy["nested", "sharpe"])` against
`r sprintf("%.3f", stats60["nested", "sharpe"])`, earned on the higher return
(`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * stats60_ccy["nested", "ann_return"])` against
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * stats60["nested", "ann_return"])`) at a slightly
higher volatility (`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * stats60_ccy["nested", "ann_vol"])`
against `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * stats60["nested", "ann_vol"])`). Neither
dominates the flat construction, which has both the higher return,
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * stats60["flat", "ann_return"])`, and the lower
volatility, `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * stats60["flat", "ann_vol"])`. The reason
the currency partition does better is the one
@sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-application gave for the class partition doing
badly: stage 1 of a currency sleeve sees its own country's equity against its
own country's government bond, which is exactly the entry the class partition
discards. What the currency partition discards
instead, the cross-country entries, is recovered in coarse form by a six-by-six
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}$, and the gap to the flat line is what that compression
costs. The partition the tree of the hierarchical-risk-parity box found in the
data is more efficient than the one the mandate asserted, and the flat problem
dominates both, which is the chapter's verdict again: on sixteen classes and sixty months the
cross-block covariances are information. The government sleeve still receives
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * colMeans(t(race60_ccy$sleeve_budget))[["government"]])`
of the currency-nested portfolio on average, so the hierarchy changed what
stage 1 could see, not what a minimum-variance top level buys.

#### Exercise 2

With inverse-variance budgets at the top, @eq-15-identity says the nested
portfolio *is* the flat portfolio on $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{B}}$, so the
check needs only the two lines that are supposed to coincide.

```{r}
#| label: sol-15-ex2
iv_line <- function(W) {                 # race() with the top-level step replaced
  paths <- lapply(oos, function(t) {
    X  <- Xm[(t - W):(t - 1), ]; Sw <- stats::cov(X)
    v  <- within_gmv(Sw, sleeves)
    s2 <- vapply(names(v), function(k)
      as.numeric(t(v[[k]]) %*% Sw[sleeves[[k]], sleeves[[k]]] %*% v[[k]]), numeric(1))
    Sb <- Sw; Sb[!same] <- 0
    list(iv = unroll((1 / s2) / sum(1 / s2), v), bd = gmv_qp(Sb))
  })
  list(max_gap = max(vapply(paths, function(p) max(abs(p$iv - p$bd)), numeric(1))),
       ret = vapply(seq_along(oos), function(i) sum(paths[[i]]$iv * Rm[oos[i], ]), numeric(1)))
}
windows <- c(36L, 60L, 120L)
iv <- lapply(windows, iv_line); names(iv) <- windows
gaps <- vapply(iv, `[[`, numeric(1), "max_gap")
stopifnot(all(gaps < 1e-10),
          max(abs(iv[["60"]]$ret - race60$ret[, "block-diagonal"])) < 1e-10)
signif(gaps, 2)
c(inverse_variance = oos_stats(iv[["60"]]$ret)[["sharpe"]],
  block_diagonal   = stats60["block-diagonal", "sharpe"])
```

The largest discrepancy in any rolling window, at any of the three estimation
windows, is `r sprintf("%.1e", max(gaps))`, and the return line at sixty months
is the block-diagonal line of @tbl-15-oos to the same precision. The
difference between the nested and block-diagonal rows of that table, which is
`r sprintf("%.3f", stats60["nested", "sharpe"] - stats60["block-diagonal", "sharpe"])`
of Sharpe ratio at sixty months, therefore measures exactly one thing: the
out-of-sample value of the $K(K-1)/2 = `r choose(length(sleeves), 2)`$
cross-sleeve covariances that stage 2 carries in $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$, because
the two constructions share stage 1, share the sleeve variances, and differ in
nothing else.

#### Exercise 3

```{r}
#| label: sol-15-ex3
hc_c <- hclust(stats::as.dist(D), method = "complete")
cl4  <- cutree(hc_c, k = 4)
stopifnot(identical(names(cl4), colnames(Re)))
xt <- table(cluster = cl4, sleeve = sleeve_of(names(cl4)))
xt

pure <- sum(apply(xt, 1, function(r) sum(r > 0) == 1L))
equity_alone <- length(unique(cl4[sleeves$equity])) == 1L &&
  sum(cl4 == cl4[["US_equity"]]) == length(sleeves$equity)
stopifnot(identical(cl4[["JP_government"]], cl4[["JP_credit"]]),
          identical(cl4[["US_government"]], cl4[["US_credit"]]),
          cl4[["JP_government"]] != cl4[["US_government"]],
          length(unique(cl4[c(paste0(c("CH", "EU", "UK"), "_government"),
                              paste0(c("CH", "EU", "UK"), "_credit"),
                              "GLOBAL_commodity")])) == 1L)
w_hrp_c <- hrp(S, colnames(Re)[hc_c$order])
sizes_single   <- sort(as.integer(table(cutree(hc, k = 4))), decreasing = TRUE)
sizes_complete <- sort(as.integer(rowSums(xt)), decreasing = TRUE)
stopifnot(sizes_single[1] > sizes_complete[1],          # single linkage chains
          eff_bets(w_hrp_c) > eff_bets(w_hrp))
c(pure_clusters = pure, equity_sleeve_recovered = equity_alone,
  largest_cluster_single_linkage = sizes_single[1],
  top_weight_single = max(w_hrp), top_weight_complete = max(w_hrp_c),
  bets_single = eff_bets(w_hrp), bets_complete = eff_bets(w_hrp_c))
```

No. Of the four clusters `r c("none", "one", "two", "three", "four")[pure + 1L]`
is pure: the five equity series form a cluster of their own, and that is the
only sleeve the tree recovers. The
fixed-income half is cut by currency, as the single-linkage order in
@sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-theory already suggested: the two Japanese
bond series are a cluster of `r sum(cl4 == cl4[["JP_government"]])`, the two
United States bond series another, and the
`r sum(cl4 == cl4[["UK_government"]]) - 1L` remaining bond series of Switzerland,
the euro area and the United Kingdom share the fourth cluster with the
commodity. Complete linkage does change the picture in one respect: single
linkage cut at four clusters gives one cluster of
`r sizes_single[1]` series and leaves `r sum(sizes_single[-1])` for the other
three (of `r paste(sizes_single[-1], collapse = ", ")`), the chaining
single linkage is prone to and the reason @raffinot2018 compares linkages at
all, whereas complete linkage produces groups of
`r paste(sizes_complete, collapse = ", ")`. The allocation it produces is more spread, with
`r sprintf("%.1f", eff_bets(w_hrp_c))` effective positions against
`r sprintf("%.1f", eff_bets(w_hrp))`, but still puts
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * max(w_hrp_c))` in `r names(which.max(w_hrp_c))`,
because the linkage changes the order of the list and not the inverse-variance
rule that bisects it.

#### Exercise 4

```{r}
#| label: sol-15-ex4
backfill <- function(W) {
  bh      <- sapply(three, proxy_by_hand, W = W)
  kept    <- gmv_qp(stats::cov(bh))                  # the package's top level
  dropped <- gmv_qp(stats::cov(bh[-(1:W), ]))        # without the back-filled months
  tibble::tibble(window = W, backfilled_share = W / nrow(bh),
                 max_move = max(abs(kept - dropped)),
                 government_kept = kept[["government"]],
                 government_dropped = dropped[["government"]],
                 vol_backfilled = stats::sd(bh[1:W, "government"]) * sqrt(12),
                 vol_rolling    = stats::sd(bh[-(1:W), "government"]) * sqrt(12))
}
bf <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c(36L, 60L, 120L), backfill))
stopifnot(abs(bf$government_kept[bf$window == 60L] - b_hand[["government"]]) < 1e-12,
          all(diff(bf$max_move) > 0),                         # the longer the window, the larger the move
          all(bf$government_kept < bf$government_dropped),    # back-fill moves budget away from government
          all(bf$vol_backfilled > bf$vol_rolling))
bf |>
  dplyr::transmute(window,
                   `back-filled share`   = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * backfilled_share),
                   `largest move`        = sprintf("%.2f pp", 100 * max_move),
                   `government, kept`    = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * government_kept),
                   `government, dropped` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * government_dropped),
                   `sleeve vol, back-filled` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * vol_backfilled),
                   `sleeve vol, rolling`     = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * vol_rolling)) |>
  kable(align = "rrrrrrr")
```

The back-fill matters most at one hundred and twenty months, where dropping it
moves a top-level weight by up to
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * bf$max_move[bf$window == 120L])` percentage points,
against `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * bf$max_move[bf$window == 60L])` at sixty and
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * bf$max_move[bf$window == 36L])` at thirty-six. The
move is proportional to the share of the history that is back-filled,
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * bf$backfilled_share[bf$window == 36L])`,
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * bf$backfilled_share[bf$window == 60L])` and
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * bf$backfilled_share[bf$window == 120L])` of the
sample: the ratio of the one to the other is between
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(bf$max_move / bf$backfilled_share))` and
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(bf$max_move / bf$backfilled_share))` at every window.
The direction is the same each time, budget moving from the government sleeve
to equity when the back-fill is kept, and the reason is what the back-filled
months contain. They are an equally weighted, buy-and-hold basket of five
unhedged government series, whose volatility is
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * bf$vol_backfilled[bf$window == 120L])` a year
against `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * bf$vol_rolling[bf$window == 120L])` for the
months the rolling minimum-variance sleeve actually ran, so every back-filled
month reports a more volatile government sleeve than the one the manager holds,
and the top level believes it in proportion to how many such months it is
shown. The longer the training period the package is given, the more of the
history it estimates the policy on is a portfolio nobody chose.
